title: 3.2.22 Plain English to Pseudocode: Data Flow Through Chained Calls
description: Turn five plain-English steps into pseudocode for two nested calls: double(5) first, addTen on what it hands back, then a Big/Small decision on the result.

planChart.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A([the program starts]) --> B[[double of 5 hands back 10]]
  B --> C[[addTen of 10 hands back 20]]
  C --> D[set result to the value addTen returned]
  D --> E{is result over 25?}
  E -- yes --> F[/print Big/]
  E -- no --> G[/print Small/]
  F --> Z([the program ends])
  G --> Z
planChart.caption: Chained calls: the inner call double(5) runs first, its answer travels into addTen, and only then does the diamond test result.

steps.title: Turn the plain-English steps into pseudocode
steps.instructions:
Here is the plan in plain English:

**1.** Call `double` with `5`. It hands back `10`.

**2.** Call `addTen` with that `10` (the value `double` just handed back). It hands back `20`.

**3.** Set `result` to the value `addTen` handed back.

**4.** If `result` is over `25`, print `Big`.

**5.** Otherwise, print `Small`.

The same plan is drawn as a flow chart above the editor (open the Flow Chart bar). You do not draw it, you read it: the two double-rail boxes are the two calls in the order they run, the diamond tests `result`, and both prints end at the same place.

In `README.md`, type these as numbered pseudocode **between the first and last line**. Number every line, including indented ones. Each keyword looks like this, in a different program:

- `SET lives TO 3` (start a value)
- `IF lives is 0` ... `END IF` (a check, with the steps inside it indented)
- `FOR EACH life IN lives` ... `END FOR` (repeat for every item)
- `PRINT lives` (show something)

Plain English is fine here. Press **Grade** above the editor: the AI reads what your steps mean and marks each Quest card green or red. Changing your text clears its marks, so press Grade again when you have finished editing.

Before you submit, trace it by hand with `5`: `double(5)` is `10`, `addTen(10)` is `20`, and `20 > 25` is false, so the program prints `Small`. If yours reaches `Big`, the calls are in the wrong order or the check tests the wrong value.
hints: The inner call comes first: `addTen` needs the number `double` hands back, so it cannot run before `double`.
The check is on `result`, after both calls, and Big and Small are two ways out of one check (an ELSE).

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your steps
aiCheck.prompt: The student was given five plain-English steps and rewrote them as numbered, step-by-step pseudocode in README.md, between a first line and a last line that were already there. The program is: function double(n) { return n * 2; } function addTen(n) { return n + 10; } const result = addTen(double(5)); if (result > 25) print "Big" else print "Small". The point is that the inner call double(5) runs first, its value (10) is handed to the outer call addTen, result is set to what addTen returns (20), and only then is result compared with 25. Judge each criterion ONLY by whether its idea is present in the student's steps, however they word it. Plain English, keywords such as SET, IF, ELSE, END IF, FOR EACH, END FOR, CALL, PRINT, or a mix of both are all fine, and so are different names, different capitalisation, and different ways to number the lines. Do not require any particular keyword. A step that is clearly aimed at the criterion is enough for 'met'. Mark a criterion 'missing' only when the idea is absent or the steps do the opposite (for example addTen running before double, or testing 20 instead of 25). Write each note for THIS student's own steps: in a not-met note, name the exact step or word in their steps that causes the problem (quote at most a few words), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected steps. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their steps satisfied it. Do not use generic praise.
